The sequence~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d}')$ can be obtained by deleting the~$1$ entry~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{i+3k}$ and the~$0$ entry~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{i+3k-1}$ in~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})$ and inserting a~$1$ entry at~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{i'+3k}$.
\item
nodes.statement_short: Two deletions and one insertion

nodes.name: Case 3: pattern generated
nodes.statement:
The deletion generates a new \emph{synchronization pattern}~$(c'_{i'+1},\ldots,c'_{i'+3k+\lceil \log k\rceil +4})$ for some~$i'$ and no \emph{synchronization pattern} is destroyed. Then the
~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d}')$ can be obtained by deleting  two~$0$ entries~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{i'+3k}$ and~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{i'+3k+1}$ in~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})$ and inserting a~$1$ entry at~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{i'+3k}$.
\item
nodes.statement_short: Two deletions of 0 entries and one insertion

nodes.name: Case 4: no change
nodes.statement: No \emph{synchronization pattern} is generated or destroyed. Then~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d}')$ can be obtained by deleting a~$0$ entry~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{j}$, where~$j$ is the location of the deletion.
nodes.statement_short: Delete one 0 entry

nodes.name: Summary of cases
nodes.statement: In a summary, in each of the above cases, a single deletion in~$\mathbf{c}$ causes at most two deletions and one insertion in~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})$.
nodes.statement_short: Each case gives at most two deletions and one insertion

nodes.name: Conclude via Lemma 6
nodes.statement: Hence~$k$ deletions in~$\mathbf{c}$ and~$\mathbf{c}'$ cause at most~$2k$ deletions and~$k$ insertions in~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})$ and~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')$ respectively. According to Lemma~\ref{lemma:bkball}, we have that~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')\in B_{3k}(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}))$ when~$\mathbf{c}'\in B_k(\mathbf{c})$. Hence Proposition~\ref{lemma:editdistance} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: $k$ deletions give $2k$ deletions and $k$ insertions; apply Lemma 6

nodes.name: Deletion index sets
nodes.statement:
We first compute the difference~$ \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{m}^{(e)}- \mathbf{c}' \cdot  \mathbf{m}^{(e)}$.
Since~$\mathbf{c}'\in B_{3k}(\mathbf{c})$, there exist two subsets~$\boldsymbol{\delta}=\{\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{3k}\}\subset \{1,\ldots,n\}$ and~$\boldsymbol{\delta}'=\{\delta'_{1},\ldots,\delta'_{3k}\}\subset \{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that deleting bits with indices~$\boldsymbol{\delta}$ and~$\boldsymbol{\delta}'$ respectively from~$\mathbf{c}$ and~$\mathbf{c}'$ result in the same length~$n-3k$ subsequence, i.e.,~$(c_i:i\notin\boldsymbol{\delta})=(c'_i:i\notin\boldsymbol{\delta'})$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix deletion index sets $\delta,\delta'$ giving a common subsequence

nodes.name: Index sets of 1 entries
nodes.statement:
Let~$\boldsymbol{\Delta}=\{i:c_i=1\}$ and~$\boldsymbol{\Delta}'=\{i:c'_i=1\}$ be the indices of~$1$ entries in~$\mathbf{c}$ and~$\mathbf{c}'$ respectively.
Let~$S_1=\boldsymbol{\Delta}\cap \boldsymbol{\delta}$ 
be the indices of~$1$ entries that are deleted in~$\mathbf{c}$. Then
$S^c_1=\boldsymbol{\Delta}\cap ([1,n]\backslash \boldsymbol{\delta})$ denotes the indices of~$1$ entries  that are not deleted. Similarly let~$S_2=\boldsymbol{\Delta}'\cap \boldsymbol{\delta}'$ and~$S^c_2=\boldsymbol{\Delta}'\cap ([1,n]\backslash \boldsymbol{\delta}')$ be the indices of $1$ entries that are deleted and not in~$\mathbf{c}'$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\Delta,\Delta'$ and deleted/kept 1-index sets $S_1,S_2,S^c_1,S^c_2$

nodes.name: Difference formula
nodes.statement:
Let the elements in~$\boldsymbol{\delta}\cup \boldsymbol{\delta'}$ be ordered by~$1\le p_1\le p_2\le\ldots\le p_{6k}\le n$. Denoting~$p_0=0$ and~$p_{6k+1}=n$, we have that
\begin{align} \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{m}^{(e)}- \mathbf{c}' \cdot  \mathbf{m}^{(e)}&=\sum_{\ell\in \boldsymbol{\Delta}}\mathbf{m}^{(e)}_\ell - \sum_{\ell\in\boldsymbol{ \Delta}'}\mathbf{m}^{(e)}_\ell
    \nonumber\\
    &=\sum_{\ell\in \boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\sum^\ell_{i=1}i^e) - \sum_{\ell\in\boldsymbol{ \Delta}'}(\sum^\ell_{i=1}i^e)\nonumber\\
    &=\sum^n_{i=1}(\sum_{\ell\in \boldsymbol{\Delta}\cap[i,n]}i^e) - \sum^n_{i=1}(\sum_{\ell\in \boldsymbol{\Delta'}\cap [i,n]}i^e)\nonumber\\
    &=\sum^n_{i=1}(|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\cap[i,n]|-|\boldsymbol{\Delta}'\cap[i,n]|)i^e \nonumber\\
    &= \sum^n_{i=1}(|S_1\cap[i,n]|+|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S_2\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|)i^e\nonumber\\
    &=\sum^{6k}_{j=0}\sum^{p_{j+1}}_{i=p_{j}+1}(|S_1\cap[i,n]|-|S_2\cap[i,n]|+|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|)i^e\nonumber\\
    &\overset{(1)}{=}\sum^{6k}_{j=0}\sum^{p_{j+1}}_{i=p_{j}+1}(|S_1\cap[p_{j+1},n]|-|S_2\cap[p_{j+1},n]|+|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|)i^e,

\end{align}
where~$(1)$ holds since there is no~$1$ entry in interval~$(p_j,p_{j+1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the parity-check difference as a sum over intervals $(p_j,p_{j+1}]$

nodes.name: Goal (1)
nodes.statement:
In the following we show
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $-1\le |S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|\le 1$ for~$i\in [1,n]$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: State the bound $|\,|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|\,|\le1$ to be shown

nodes.name: Goal (2)
nodes.statement:
For each interval~$(p_j,p_{j+1}]$,~$j=0,\ldots,6k$, we have either~$|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|\le 0$ for all~$i\in (p_j,p_{j+1}]$ or
$|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|\ge 0$
for all~$i\in (p_j,p_{j+1}]$.
nodes.statement_short: State the constant-sign property on each interval

nodes.name: Proof of (1)
nodes.statement:
\emph{Proof of (1)}: 
Since deleting bits with indices~$\boldsymbol{\delta}$ in~$\mathbf{c}$ and deleting bits with indices~$\boldsymbol{\delta'}$ in~$\mathbf{c}'$ result in the same subsequence.
Hence for every~$i\in S^c_1$, there is a unique corresponding index~$i'\in S^c_2$ such that the two~$1$ entries~$c_i$ and~$c'_{i'}$ end in the same location after deletions, i.e.,~$i-|\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap [1,i-1]|=i'-|\boldsymbol{\delta}'\cap [1,i'-1]|$. This implies that~$|i'-i|\le 3k$. 
Fix integers~$i$ and~$i'$. Then by definition of~$i$ and~$i'$, for every~$x\in S^c_1\cap [i+1,n]$ there is a unique corresponding~$y\in S^c_2\cap[i'+,n]$ such that the two~$1$ entries~$c_x$ and~$c'_y$ end in the same location after deletions. Hence we have that~$|S^c_1\cap[i+1,n]|=|S^c_2\cap[i'+1,n]|$ and that~$|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|=|S^c_2\cap[i',n]|$. Without loss of generality assume that~$i'\ge i$. Then,
\begin{align*}
    |S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|&=|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i',n]|-
    |S^c_2\cap[i+1,i']|\\
    &=-|S^c_2\cap[i+1,i']|\\
    &\overset{(a)}{\ge} -|S^c_2\cap[i+1,i+3k]|\\
    &\overset{(b)}{\ge} -1,
\end{align*}
where~$(a)$ follows from the fact that~$|i'-i|\le 3k$ and~$(b)$ follows from the fact that~$\mathbf{c},\mathbf{c}'\in\mathcal{R}_{3k}$. Similarly, when~$i'\le i$, we have that~$|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|\le 1$. This completes the proof of~$(1)$
nodes.statement_short: Prove the $\pm1$ bound via the matching of surviving 1 entries

nodes.name: Matching of surviving 1's
nodes.statement:
Since deleting bits with indices~$\boldsymbol{\delta}$ in~$\mathbf{c}$ and deleting bits with indices~$\boldsymbol{\delta'}$ in~$\mathbf{c}'$ result in the same subsequence.
Hence for every~$i\in S^c_1$, there is a unique corresponding index~$i'\in S^c_2$ such that the two~$1$ entries~$c_i$ and~$c'_{i'}$ end in the same location after deletions, i.e.,~$i-|\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap [1,i-1]|=i'-|\boldsymbol{\delta}'\cap [1,i'-1]|$. This implies that~$|i'-i|\le 3k$.
nodes.statement_short: Surviving 1 entries match with index shift at most $3k$

nodes.name: Tail counts agree
nodes.statement: Fix integers~$i$ and~$i'$. Then by definition of~$i$ and~$i'$, for every~$x\in S^c_1\cap [i+1,n]$ there is a unique corresponding~$y\in S^c_2\cap[i'+,n]$ such that the two~$1$ entries~$c_x$ and~$c'_y$ end in the same location after deletions. Hence we have that~$|S^c_1\cap[i+1,n]|=|S^c_2\cap[i'+1,n]|$ and that~$|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|=|S^c_2\cap[i',n]|$.
nodes.statement_short: Matched tails have equal counts

nodes.name: Bound using R_3k
nodes.statement:
Without loss of generality assume that~$i'\ge i$. Then,
\begin{align*}
    |S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|&=|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i',n]|-
    |S^c_2\cap[i+1,i']|\\
    &=-|S^c_2\cap[i+1,i']|\\
    &\overset{(a)}{\ge} -|S^c_2\cap[i+1,i+3k]|\\
    &\overset{(b)}{\ge} -1,
\end{align*}
where~$(a)$ follows from the fact that~$|i'-i|\le 3k$ and~$(b)$ follows from the fact that~$\mathbf{c},\mathbf{c}'\in\mathcal{R}_{3k}$. Similarly, when~$i'\le i$, we have that~$|S^c_1\cap[i,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i,n]|\le 1$. This completes the proof of~$(1)$
nodes.statement_short: Use $|i'-i|\le3k$ and the $\mathcal{R}_{3k}$ spacing to get the bound

nodes.name: Proof of (2)
nodes.statement_short: Prove sign-constancy on each interval by contradiction

nodes.name: Assume sign change
nodes.statement_short: Assume a sign change at $i_1<i_2$ in one interval

nodes.name: First deletion-count inequality
nodes.statement:
By symmetry it can be assumed that~$|S^c_1\cap[i_1,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i_1,n]=-1$ and~$|S^c_1\cap[i_2,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i_2,n]|=1$. Note that~$|S^c_1|=|S^c_2|$ and there exists a one-to-one correspondence between the elements in~$S^c_1$ and the elements in~$S^c_2$. Hence from~$|S^c_1\cap[i_1,n]|-|S^c_2\cap[i_1,n]=-1$, there exist two integers~$x\in S^c_1\cap[i_1-1,n]$
and~$y\in S^c_2\cap[i_1,n]$ such that the two~$1$ entries~$c_x$ and~$c'_y$ are in the same location after deletions, i.e.,~$x-|\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap[1,x-1]|=y-|\boldsymbol{\delta}'\cap[1,y-1]|$. Therefore, we have that
\begin{align*}
    i_1-|\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap[1,i_1-1]|>&i_1-1-|\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap[1,i_1-1]|\\
    \ge&x-|\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap[1,x-1]|\\
    =&y-|\boldsymbol{\delta}'\cap[1,y-1]|\\
    \ge& i_1-|\boldsymbol{\delta}'\cap[1,i_1-1]|,
\end{align*}
which implies that
\begin{align} |\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap[1,i_1-1]|<|\boldsymbol{\delta}'\cap[1,i_1-1]|.
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Derive $|\delta\cap[1,i_1-1]|<|\delta'\cap[1,i_1-1]|$

nodes.name: Second deletion-count inequality
nodes.statement_short: Derive the reverse inequality at $i_2$

nodes.name: Combine inequalities
nodes.statement:
Eq.~\eqref{equation:contradiction1} and Eq.~\eqref{equation:contradiction2} implies that
\begin{align} |\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap[1,i_2-1]|-|\boldsymbol{\delta}\cap[1,i_1-1]|\ge &
|\boldsymbol{\delta}'\cap[1,i_2-1]|+1-|\boldsymbol{\delta}'\cap[1,i_1-1]|+1\nonumber\\
\ge & 2.
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: At least two deletions between $i_1$ and $i_2$

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement_short: At most one deletion lies there, contradiction; (2) holds

nodes.name: Define s_i
nodes.statement_short: Define $s_i$

nodes.name: Sign of s_i constant on intervals
nodes.statement:
Note that~$|S_1\cap[i,n]|-|S_2\cap[i,n]|=|S_1\cap[p_{j+1},n]|-|S_2\cap[p_{j+1},n]|$ for~$i\in (p_j,p_{j+1}]$.
Hence from~$(1)$ and~$(2)$ it follows that for each interval~$(p_j,p_{j+1}]$,~$j\in\{0,\ldots,6k\}$, either~$s_i\ge 0$ for all~$i\in (p_j,p_{j+1}]$ or~$s_i\le 0$ for all~$i\in (p_j,p_{j+1}]$.
nodes.statement_short: From (1) and (2), $s_i$ has constant sign on each interval

nodes.name: Sign vector x
nodes.statement_short: Write the difference as a signed sum with signs $x_j$

nodes.name: Linear system
nodes.statement_short: Equal checks give a linear system $A\mathbf{x}=0$

nodes.name: A must vanish
nodes.statement_short: Show $A$ must be zero

nodes.name: Nonzero submatrix B
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to nonzero columns to get $B\mathbf{x}'=0$

nodes.name: Vandermonde determinant
nodes.statement:
By the multi-linearity of the determinant, 
\begin{align}
\det(B)=&\sum_{i_1\in (p_{j_1-1},p_{j_1}],\ldots,i_M\in (p_{j_Q-1},p_{j_Q}]}\det \begin{pmatrix} |s_{i_1}|i^0_1&\ldots&|s_{i_Q}|i^0_Q\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ |s_{i_1}|i_1^{Q-1}&|s_{i_Q}|\ldots&i_Q^{Q-1} \end{pmatrix}\nonumber\\
=&\sum_{i_1\in (p_{j_1-1},p_{j_1}],\ldots,i_Q\in (p_{j_{Q-1}},p_{j_Q}]}[\prod^Q_{q=1} |s_{i_q}| \prod_{1\le m<\ell \le Q}(i_{\ell}-i_{m})]
\end{align}
is positive since~$i_{\ell}>i_{m}$ for~$m>\ell$
and for~$i_1\in (p_{j_1-1},p_{j_1}],\ldots,i_Q\in (p_{j_Q-1},p_{j_Q}]$. Note that all the columns of~$B$ are nonzero.
nodes.statement_short: Multilinearity and Vandermonde give $\det B>0$

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Therefore, the linear equation~$B\boldsymbol{x}'=0$ does not have nonzero solutions, contradicting to the fact that~$\boldsymbol{x}'\in\{-1,1\}^Q$.
nodes.statement_short: No nonzero $\pm1$ solution exists, contradiction

nodes.name: Conclude c = c'
nodes.statement_short: $A=0$ forces $\Delta=\Delta'$, hence $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c}'$

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 1
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{lemma:editdistance} we have that~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')\in B_{3k}(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}))$. Hence~$(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')_i,\ldots,\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')_n)\in B_{3k}((\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_i,\ldots,\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_n))$.
nodes.statement_short: Synchronization vectors lie in a radius-$3k$ ball

nodes.name: Difference below modulus
nodes.statement:
This implies that~$||\boldsymbol{\Delta}\cap[i,n]|-|\boldsymbol{\Delta}'\cap[i,n]||\le 3k$, where~~$\boldsymbol{\Delta}=\{i:\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_i=1\}$ and~$\boldsymbol{\Delta}'=\{i:\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')_i=1\}$. Hence According to Eq.~\eqref{equation:difference}, we have that
\begin{align} |\mathbbold{1}_{sync}( \mathbf{c}) \cdot \mathbf{m}^{(e)}- \mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}') \cdot  \mathbf{m}^{(e)}| =&|\sum^n_{i=1}(|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\cap[i,n]|-|\boldsymbol{\Delta}'\cap[i,n]|)i^e|,\nonumber\\
    \le&\sum^n_{i=1}3ki^e\nonumber\\
    <& 3kn^{e+1}.
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the parity-check difference by $3kn^{e+1}$

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 2
nodes.statement: If~$f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}))=f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}'))$, then~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}( \mathbf{c}) \cdot \mathbf{m}^{(e)}\equiv \mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}') \cdot  \mathbf{m}^{(e)} \bmod{3kn^{e+1}}$, which from Eq.~\eqref{equation:upperboundg} implies that~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}( \mathbf{c}) \cdot \mathbf{m}^{(e)}= \mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}') \cdot  \mathbf{m}^{(e)}$.  Since~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')\in B_{3k}(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}))$ and $\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}),\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')\in\mathcal{R}_{3k}$, from Proposition \ref{lemma:vtextension} we conclude that~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})=\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')$. Hence Lemma~\ref{lemma:syncvector} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Equal residues give equal checks; Proposition 2 concludes

nodes.name: Differences are nonzero
nodes.statement:
We are now ready to prove Lemma~ef{lemma:protectingpattern}.
We have shown in Lemma~ef{lemma:syncvector} that~$f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}))
e f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}'))$ for~$\mathbf{c}'\in B_k(\mathbf{c}) ackslash \{\mathbf{c}\}$. Hence

ewline$|M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})))-M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')))|
e 0$ (recall Eq.~\eqref{equation:Mfunction} for definition of function~$M(\mathbf{v})$) for~$\mathbf{c}'\in B_k(\mathbf{c}) ackslash \{\mathbf{c}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 1, $M(f)$ differences are nonzero on the ball

nodes.name: Divisor bound
nodes.statement_short: Each difference has $2^{o(\log n)}$ divisors

nodes.name: Divisor set P(c)
nodes.statement_short: Define the set of all such divisors

nodes.name: Choose a non-divisor
nodes.statement_short: $|\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{c})|\le 2^{2k\log n+o(\log n)}$, so a small non-divisor $p(\mathbf{c})$ exists

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Hence, if~$M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')))\equiv M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})))\bmod p(\mathbf{c})$ and~$\mathbf{c}'\in B_k(\mathbf{c})$, we have that~$p(\mathbf{c})||M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c}')))-M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})))|$ and thus~$\mathbf{c}'=\mathbf{c}$. 
This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:protectingpattern}.
nodes.statement_short: Congruence mod $p(\mathbf{c})$ forces $\mathbf{c}'=\mathbf{c}$

nodes.name: Reduce to blocks
nodes.statement:
Since~$\mathbf{c}_{t_j}=\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_j}=1$ for~$j\in[1,J]$, it suffices to show that~$\mathbf{a}_j$,~$j\in[0,J]$ can be recovered
correctly.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to recover each block $\mathbf{a}_j$

nodes.name: Blocks from hashes
nodes.statement: Furthermore, note that $(d_{t_{j}+1},\ldots,d_{t_{j+1}-k-1})$ is a length~$|\mathbf{a}_j|-k$ subsequence of~$\mathbf{a}_j$, hence ~$\mathbf{a}_j$ can be correctly found given~$\mathbf{b}_j$ and~$H(\mathbf{a}_j)$,~$j\in [0.J]$.
nodes.statement_short: Each block is recovered from its subsequence and $H(\mathbf{a}_j)$

nodes.name: Reduce to 2k block errors
nodes.statement: It is then left to recover~$H(\mathbf{a}_j)$ for~$j\in [0,J]$. To this end, we show that there are at most~$2k$ indices~$j$, such that~$\mathbf{a}'_j\ne \mathbf{a}_j$. Then there are at most~$2k$ symbol errors in the sequence~$(H(\mathbf{a}_0),\ldots,H(\mathbf{a}_J))$, which can be corrected given the Reed-Solomon code redundancy~$Hash_k(\mathbf{c})$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show at most $2k$ blocks are misidentified

nodes.name: Indices after deletion
nodes.statement: Let~$i_j$,~$j\in[1,J]$ be the index of~$\mathbf{c}_{t_j}$ in~$\mathbf{d}$ after deletions, where~$i_j=-1$ if~$\mathbf{c}_{t_j}$ is deleted. Let~$i_0=0$ and~$i_{J+1}=n+1-k$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce positions $i_j$ of the synchronization 1's in $\mathbf{d}$

nodes.name: Good intervals
nodes.statement: The interval~$[i_j,i_{j+1}]$,~$j\in [0.J]$ is called \emph{good} if~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})_{i_j}=\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})_{i_{j+1}}=1$ and~$i_{j+1}-i_j=t_{j+1}-t_{j}$. Note that by definition,~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})_{i_0}=\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})_{i_{J+1}}=1$. Since~$\mathbf{d}_{i_j}=\mathbf{c}_{t_j}$ and~$i_j\in [t_j-k,t_j]$ for~$j\in[0,J]$, we have that~$\mathbf{a}'_{j}=\mathbf{a}_j$ if the interval~$[i_j,i_{j+1}]$ is~\emph{good}.
nodes.statement_short: Define good intervals; good intervals give correct blocks

nodes.name: A deletion destroys at most 2 good intervals
nodes.statement:
Now we show that a deletion can destroy at most~$2$ \emph{good} intervals. 
Suppose that the deletion occurs in interval~$[t_j,t_{j+1}]$ in~$\mathbf{c}$ for some~$j$. 
If the deletion turns the~$1$ entry~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_j}$ to~$0$, then the~$1$ entry~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_{j+1}}$ stays. As a result, at most two \emph{good} intervals~$[i_{j-1},i_j]$ and~$[i_{j},i_{j+1}]$ are destroyed. Similarly, if the deletion turns~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_{j+1}}$ to~$0$, then at most two \emph{good} intervals~$[i_j,i_{j+1}]$ and~$[i_{j+1},i_{j+2}]$ are destroyed. If both~$1$ entries~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_j}$ and~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_{j+1}}$ are not affected, then the deletion destroys only one \emph{good} interval~$[i_{j},i_{j+1}]$. In conclusion, a deletion affects at most two~\emph{good} intervals and thus at most~$2k$ block errors~$\mathbf{a}'_j\ne\mathbf{a}_j$ occur.
nodes.statement_short: Show each deletion destroys at most two good intervals

nodes.name: Locate deletion
nodes.statement: Suppose that the deletion occurs in interval~$[t_j,t_{j+1}]$ in~$\mathbf{c}$ for some~$j$.
nodes.statement_short: Place the deletion in $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$

nodes.name: Endpoint affected
nodes.statement: If the deletion turns the~$1$ entry~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_j}$ to~$0$, then the~$1$ entry~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_{j+1}}$ stays. As a result, at most two \emph{good} intervals~$[i_{j-1},i_j]$ and~$[i_{j},i_{j+1}]$ are destroyed. Similarly, if the deletion turns~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_{j+1}}$ to~$0$, then at most two \emph{good} intervals~$[i_j,i_{j+1}]$ and~$[i_{j+1},i_{j+2}]$ are destroyed.
nodes.statement_short: If an endpoint 1 is destroyed, two intervals affected

nodes.name: Endpoints unaffected
nodes.statement: If both~$1$ entries~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_j}$ and~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{t_{j+1}}$ are not affected, then the deletion destroys only one \emph{good} interval~$[i_{j},i_{j+1}]$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise only one interval affected

nodes.name: At most 2k block errors
nodes.statement: In conclusion, a deletion affects at most two~\emph{good} intervals and thus at most~$2k$ block errors~$\mathbf{a}'_j\ne\mathbf{a}_j$ occur.
nodes.statement_short: Hence at most $2k$ block errors

nodes.name: Conclude Lemma 3
nodes.statement: Therefore, the sequence~$\mathbf{c}$ can be recovered and this proves Lemma~\ref{lemma:recoverforkdense}.
nodes.statement_short: Reed-Solomon corrects the errors; Lemma 3 follows

nodes.name: Synchronization positions
nodes.statement:
Let 
the locations of the~$1$ entries in~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})$ be~$t_1<\ldots<t_J$. Let~$t_0=0$ and~$t_{J+1}=n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the positions $t_i$

nodes.name: Reduce to gap bound
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that~$t_{i+1}-t_i\le B+R+1=L+1$ for any~$i\in [0,J]$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to bound gaps by $L+1$

nodes.name: Apply Properties 2 and 1
nodes.statement:
According to Property~$2$, there exists an index~$j^*\in [t_i,t_i+R-3k-\lceil \log k\rceil-4]$, such that~$(c_{m},c_{m+1},\ldots,c_{m+\lceil\log k\rceil+4})\ne \boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ for every~$m\in [j^*,j^*+3k-1]$. 
According to Property~$1$, there exists an integer~$x\in [j^*+1,j^*+B]$ such that ~$(c_{x},c_{x+1},\ldots,c_{x+\lceil\log k\rceil+4})= \boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$.
nodes.statement_short: Find a run-free window at $j^*$ and a 1-run within $B$ after it

nodes.name: First run after j*
nodes.statement: Let~$\ell=\min_{x\ge j^*,(c_{x},c_{x+1},\ldots,c_{x+\lceil\log k\rceil+4})= \boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}}x$. Then we have that~$\ell\in [j^*+1,j^*+B]$ and that~$(c_{m},c_{m+1},\ldots,c_{m+\lceil\log k\rceil+4})\ne \boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ for every~$m\in [j^*,\ell)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the first run $\ell$ after $j^*$

nodes.name: Synchronization 1 at l
nodes.statement: By definition of~$j^*$, we have that~$\ell-j^*\ge 3k$. Since~$c_{\ell},c_{\ell+1},\ldots,c_{\ell+\lceil\log k\rceil+4})= \boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$, we have that~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})_{\ell}=1$.
nodes.statement_short: $\ell-j^*\ge3k$, so position $\ell$ is a synchronization 1

nodes.name: Gap bound
nodes.statement:
Therefore, we conclude that
\begin{align*}
t_{i+1}-t_i&\le \ell-t_i\\
&\le j^*+B-t_i\\
&\le R+B+1\\
&=L+1
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Gap $\le R+B+1=L+1$

nodes.name: Compression map phi
nodes.statement:
We first show that
every sequence~$\mathbf{b}\in\{0,1\}^{B}$ containing no consecutive~$\lceil \log k\rceil+5$~$1$'s can be uniquely represented by a sequence~$\phi(\mathbf{b})$ of length~$B-\lceil \log n\rceil-2\lceil \log k\rceil-12$.
Split~$\mathbf{b}$ into~$2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil$ blocks of length~$(\lceil \log k\rceil+5)$. Since each block is not~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$, it can be represented by a symbol of alphabet size~$2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}-1$. Therefore, the sequence~$\mathbf{b}$ can be uniquely represented by a sequence~$\mathbf{v}$ of~$2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil$ symbols, each having alphabet size~$2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}-1$. Convert~$\mathbf{v}$ into a binary sequence~$\phi (\mathbf{b})$. Then $\phi(\mathbf{b})$ can be represented by bits with length 
\begin{align} D\triangleq & \log_2 (2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}-1)^{2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil} \nonumber\\
= &\log_2 (1-1/2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5})^{2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil} + (\lceil \log k\rceil+5)2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil\nonumber\\
= &16\log_2 (1-1/2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5})^{2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}} \lceil \log n \rceil+B \nonumber\\
\overset{(a)}{\le}&-16\log_2 e \lceil \log n \rceil+B\nonumber\\
\le&B-16\lceil \log n\rceil\nonumber\\
\le&B-\lceil \log n\rceil-2\lceil \log k\rceil-12,
\end{align}
where~$(a)$ follows from the fact that the function~$(1-1/x)^x$ is increasing in~$x$ for~$x>1$ and that~$\lim_{x\rightarrow \infty}(1-1/x)^x=1/e$.
Therefore,~$\phi(\mathbf{b})$ can be represented by~$B-\lceil \log n\rceil-2\lceil \log k\rceil-12$ bits.

For a sequence~$\mathbf{c}\in\{0,1\}^n$, the encoding procedure for computing~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$ is as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Run-free length-$B$ windows compress via $\phi$ by $\lceil\log n\rceil+2\lceil\log k\rceil+12$ bits

nodes.name: Symbolize blocks
nodes.statement:
We first show that
every sequence~$\mathbf{b}\in\{0,1\}^{B}$ containing no consecutive~$\lceil \log k\rceil+5$~$1$'s can be uniquely represented by a sequence~$\phi(\mathbf{b})$ of length~$B-\lceil \log n\rceil-2\lceil \log k\rceil-12$.
Split~$\mathbf{b}$ into~$2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil$ blocks of length~$(\lceil \log k\rceil+5)$. Since each block is not~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$, it can be represented by a symbol of alphabet size~$2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Split a run-free window into blocks, each a symbol of alphabet $2^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}-1$

nodes.name: Length of phi(b)
nodes.statement:
Therefore, the sequence~$\mathbf{b}$ can be uniquely represented by a sequence~$\mathbf{v}$ of~$2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil$ symbols, each having alphabet size~$2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}-1$. Convert~$\mathbf{v}$ into a binary sequence~$\phi (\mathbf{b})$. Then $\phi(\mathbf{b})$ can be represented by bits with length 
\begin{align} D\triangleq & \log_2 (2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}-1)^{2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil} \nonumber\\
= &\log_2 (1-1/2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5})^{2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil} + (\lceil \log k\rceil+5)2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+9}\lceil \log n \rceil\nonumber\\
= &16\log_2 (1-1/2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5})^{2^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}} \lceil \log n \rceil+B \nonumber\\
\overset{(a)}{\le}&-16\log_2 e \lceil \log n \rceil+B\nonumber\\
\le&B-16\lceil \log n\rceil\nonumber\\
\le&B-\lceil \log n\rceil-2\lceil \log k\rceil-12,
\end{align}
where~$(a)$ follows from the fact that the function~$(1-1/x)^x$ is increasing in~$x$ for~$x>1$ and that~$\lim_{x\rightarrow \infty}(1-1/x)^x=1/e$.
Therefore,~$\phi(\mathbf{b})$ can be represented by~$B-\lceil \log n\rceil-2\lceil \log k\rceil-12$ bits.
nodes.statement_short: Binary conversion saves at least $16\lceil\log n\rceil$ bits

nodes.name: Encoding procedure intro
nodes.statement_short: Announce the encoding procedure for $T_1$

nodes.name: Encoding: initialization
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Initialization:} Let~$T_1(\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{c}$.
    Append~$\boldsymbol{1}^{2\lceil \log k\rceil+10}$ to the end of the sequence~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$. Let~$i=1$ and~$n'=n$. Go to Step~$1$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Append a run of ones; set $i=1$, $n'=n$

nodes.name: Encoding Step 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 1:} If~$(c_{j},c_{j+1},\ldots,c_{j+\lceil \log k\rceil+4})\ne \boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$ for every~$j\in [i,i+B-\lceil \log k\rceil-5]$, go to Step 2. Else go to Step~$4$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Test whether the window at $i$ lacks a 1-run

nodes.name: Encoding Step 2
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 2:} If~$i\le n'-B+1$,
    delete~$(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{i},\ldots,$ $T_1(\mathbf{c})_{i+B-1})$ from~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$ and  append~$(i,\phi(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{i},\ldots,T_1(\mathbf{c})_{i+B-1}),0,$ $\boldsymbol{1}^{2\lceil \log k\rceil+10},0)$ to the end of~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$. 
    Let~$n'=n'-B$ and~$i=1$. Go to Step~$1$.
    Else go to Step~$3$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Delete the run-free window and append its index and compression

nodes.name: Encoding Step 3
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 3:} Delete~$(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{i},\ldots,$ $T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n'})$ from~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$ and  append~$(i,\phi(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{i},\ldots,T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n'},\boldsymbol{0}^{i+B-n'-1}),0,$
    
    $\boldsymbol{1}^{2\lceil \log k\rceil+10-(i+B-n'-1)},0)$ to the end of~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$. 
    Let~$n'=i-1$ and~$i=1$. Go to Step~$1$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Handle a run-free tail window

nodes.name: Encoding Step 4
nodes.statement_short: Advance $i$ or output

nodes.name: Length invariant
nodes.statement:
It can be seen that the length of~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$ keeps constant and is~$n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+10$.
The integer~$n'$ is defined such that~$(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,$ $ T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+10})$ are the appended bits and~$(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{1},\ldots,T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n'})$ are the remaining bits in~$\mathbf{c}$ after the deleting operations in Step~$2$ and Step~$3$. The appended bits are not deleted in the procedure. Note that~$(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,$ $ T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n'+\lceil \log k\rceil+5})=\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$. Hence in Step~$3$, the integer~$i$ satisfies~$1\le i+B-n'-1\le \lceil \log k\rceil+4$ and the appended bits~$\boldsymbol{1}^{2\lceil \log k\rceil+10-(i+B-n'-1)}$ has length at least~$\lceil \log k\rceil+6$.
nodes.statement_short: Length stays $n+2\lceil\log k\rceil+10$; appended bits are never deleted

nodes.name: Complexity
nodes.statement: Since either~$i$ increases from~$1$ to~$n'$ or~$n'$ decreases by~$B$ in each step.  The algorithm terminates within~$O(n^2)$ times of Step~$1$, Step~$2$ and Step~$3$. Since it takes~$O(B\log k)$ to check if a subsequence is an all~$1$'s vector. The total complexity is~$O(n^2k\log n\log^2 k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Termination and $O(n^2k\log n\log^2k)$ complexity

nodes.name: Property 1 holds
nodes.statement:
We now show that the output sequence~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$.
Note that for any~$i\in [1,n']$, there exists some~$j\in [i,i+B-\lceil \log k\rceil-5]$ such that~$T_1(\mathbf{c})_{j}=T_1(\mathbf{c})_{j+1}=\ldots=T_1(\mathbf{c})_{j+\lceil \log k \rceil+4}=1$. Otherwise~$T_1(\mathbf{c})_i$ is deleted in Step~$2$ or Step~$3$. 
Moreover, the distance between two consecutive patterns~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$ after position~$n'$ is at most~$B-\lceil \log k\rceil-5$.   
Hence the sequence~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the output satisfies Property 1

nodes.name: Remaining part
nodes.statement: Note that for any~$i\in [1,n']$, there exists some~$j\in [i,i+B-\lceil \log k\rceil-5]$ such that~$T_1(\mathbf{c})_{j}=T_1(\mathbf{c})_{j+1}=\ldots=T_1(\mathbf{c})_{j+\lceil \log k \rceil+4}=1$. Otherwise~$T_1(\mathbf{c})_i$ is deleted in Step~$2$ or Step~$3$.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining bits have runs within $B$

nodes.name: Appended part
nodes.statement: Moreover, the distance between two consecutive patterns~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$ after position~$n'$ is at most~$B-\lceil \log k\rceil-5$.
nodes.statement_short: Appended bits have runs within $B$

nodes.name: Conclude Property 1
nodes.statement: Hence the sequence~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: Property 1 holds

nodes.name: Ending run
nodes.statement: It can be seen that when the inserting operation in Step~$2$ or Step~$3$ does not occur, the we have that~$(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n+\lceil \log k\rceil+6},\ldots,$ $T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+10})=\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$. If the insertion operation in Step~$2$ or Step~$3$ occurs, then we have that~$(T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n+\lceil \log k\rceil+5},\ldots,$ $T_1(\mathbf{c})_{n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+9})=\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$.
nodes.statement_short: The output ends with a run of ones in one of two positions

nodes.name: Decoding procedure intro
nodes.statement_short: Announce the decoder

nodes.name: Decoding: initialization
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Initialization:} Let~$\mathbf{c}=T_1(\mathbf{c})$ and go to Step~$1$. 
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Start from $T_1(\mathbf{c})$

nodes.name: Decoding Step 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 1:} If~$c_{n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+10}=0$, find the length~$\ell$ of the~$1$ run that ends with~$c_{n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+9}$. let~$i$ be the decimal representation of $(c_{n+4\lceil \log k\rceil+21-B-\ell},c_{n+4\lceil \log k\rceil+22-B-\ell},\ldots,$ 
    $c_{n+4\lceil \log k\rceil+20-B-\ell+\lceil \log n\rceil})$. 
    Let~$\mathbf{b}$ be the sequence obtained by computing $\phi^{-1}(c_{n+4\lceil \log k\rceil+21-B-\ell+\lceil \log n\rceil},$ 
    $c_{n+4\lceil \log k\rceil+22-B-\ell+\lceil \log n\rceil},\ldots,c_{n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+8-\ell})$, where the function~$\phi$ is defined in the paragraph before Eq.~\eqref{equation:lengthofphib} and is invertible,
    Note that the length of~$\mathbf{b}$ is~$B$.
    
    
    
    Delete~$(c_{n+4\lceil \log k\rceil+21-B-\ell},$ $c_{n+4\lceil \log k\rceil+22-B-\ell},$ $\ldots,c_{n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+10})$ from~$\mathbf{c}$ and insert~$(\mathbf{b}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{b}_{B-2\lceil \log k\rceil-10+\ell})$ at location~$i$ of~$\mathbf{c}$.
    Repeat. 
    Else delete~$c_{n+1},\ldots,c_{n+2\lceil \log k\rceil+10}$ and
    output~$\mathbf{c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Read index and $\phi$-encoding, reinsert the window, repeat

nodes.name: Decoder termination
nodes.statement: Note that in the encoding procedure, every appended subsequence has length~$B-2\lceil \log k\rceil-10+\ell$ and ends with a~$0$. Hence the algorithm stops when all the subsequences appended in Step~$2$ or Step~$3$ are deleted.
nodes.statement_short: Decoder stops once all appended parts are removed

nodes.name: Decoder reverses encoder
nodes.statement:
Moreover, the encoding procedure consists of a series of deleting and appending operations. The decoding procedure exactly reverses the series of operations in the encoding procedure. Specifically,
let~$T_{1,i}(\mathbf{c})$,~$i\in [0,I]$ be the sequence~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$ obtained after the~$i$-th deleting and appending operation in the encoding procedure, where~$I$ is the number of deleting and appending operations in total in the encoding procedure. We have that~$T_{1,0}(\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{c}$ and that~$T_{1,I}(\mathbf{c})$ is the final output~$T_{1}(\mathbf{c})$. Then the decoding procedure obtains~$T_{1,I-i}(\mathbf{c})$,~$i\in [0,I]$ after the~$i$-th deleting and inserting operation. Hence we get the output~$T_{1,I-I}(\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{c}$ in the decoding procedure.
nodes.statement_short: Decoding reverses each encoding operation, recovering $\mathbf{c}$

nodes.name: Encoding procedure intro
nodes.statement_short: Announce the encoder for $T_2$

nodes.name: Encoding: initialization
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Initialization:} Let~$T_2(\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{c}$.
    Append~$0$ to the end of the sequence~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$. Find the smallest~$i\in [1,3k]$ such that~$T_2(\mathbf{c})_i=T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+1}=\ldots=T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+\lceil \log k \rceil +4}=1$. Delete~$(T_2(\mathbf{c})_i,\ldots,T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})$ from~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$ and append~$(i,\boldsymbol{0}^{\lceil \log k\rceil +3-\lceil \log (3k) \rceil})$ to the end of~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$. Let~$n'=3k-1$ and~$i=1$.
    Go to Step~$1$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Remove the first long 1-run and append its index

nodes.name: Encoding Step 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 1:} If~$i\le n'-\lceil \log k \rceil-4$ and~$T_2(\mathbf{c})_i=T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+1}=\ldots=T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+\lceil \log k \rceil +4}=1$, 
    delete~$(T_2(\mathbf{c})_i,\ldots,T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})$ from~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$ and  append~$(i,\boldsymbol{0}^{\lceil \log k \rceil+5-\lceil \log (3k) \rceil},1)$ to the end of~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$. Let~$n'=n'-\lceil \log k\rceil -5$ and~$i=1$. Repeat.
    Else go to Step~$2$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Remove further long 1-runs, appending their indices

nodes.name: Encoding Step 2
nodes.statement_short: Advance $i$ or output

nodes.name: Length invariant
nodes.statement_short: Length is $3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+3$; appended bits are kept

nodes.name: Complexity
nodes.statement: Since either~$i$ increases from~$1$ to~$n'$ or~$n'$ decreases in each step. The algorithm terminates within~$O(k^2)$ times of Step~$1$ and Step~$2$. Since it takes~$O(\log k)$ to check if a subsequence is an all~$1$'s vector. The total complexity is~$O(k^2\log k)$.
nodes.statement_short: $O(k^2\log k)$ complexity

nodes.name: No long 1-runs
nodes.statement:
We now show that~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$ contains no~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$ patterns. According to the encoding procedure, for~$i\in [1,n']$, we have that~$(T_2(\mathbf{c})_i,\ldots,T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+\lceil \log k\rceil+4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$. Furthermore, the distance between two consecutive~$0$ entries after position~$n'$ is at most~$\lceil \log 3k\rceil+1$. Hence for any~$i\in [n'+1,3k-1]$, we have that
~$(T_2(\mathbf{c})_i,\ldots,T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+\lceil \log k\rceil+4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$. Therefore,~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$ does not contain~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$ patterns.
nodes.statement_short: Show $T_2(\mathbf{c})$ has no run of $\lceil\log k\rceil+5$ ones

nodes.name: Remaining part
nodes.statement: According to the encoding procedure, for~$i\in [1,n']$, we have that~$(T_2(\mathbf{c})_i,\ldots,T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+\lceil \log k\rceil+4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$.
nodes.statement_short: No long run in the remaining bits

nodes.name: Appended part
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, the distance between two consecutive~$0$ entries after position~$n'$ is at most~$\lceil \log 3k\rceil+1$. Hence for any~$i\in [n'+1,3k-1]$, we have that
~$(T_2(\mathbf{c})_i,\ldots,T_2(\mathbf{c})_{i+\lceil \log k\rceil+4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$.
nodes.statement_short: Zeros in appended part are dense

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore,~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$ does not contain~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k\rceil+5}$ patterns.
nodes.statement_short: No long 1-run

nodes.name: Decoding procedure intro
nodes.statement:
To show that~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$ is decodable,
we present the following procedure that recovers~$\mathbf{c}$ from~$T_2(\mathbf{c})$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Announce the decoder

nodes.name: Decoding: initialization
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Initialization:} Let~$\mathbf{c}=T_2(\mathbf{c})$ and go to Step~$1$. 
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Start from $T_2(\mathbf{c})$

nodes.name: Decoding Step 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 1:} If~$c_{3k+\lceil \log k\rceil+3}=1$, let~$i$ be the decimal representation of~$(c_{3k-1},c_{3k},\ldots,c_{3k+\lceil \log 3k \rceil-2})$. 
    Delete~$(c_{3k-1},c_{3k},$ $\ldots,c_{3k+\lceil \log k\rceil+3})$ from~$\mathbf{c}$ and insert~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil+5}$ at location~$i$ of~$\mathbf{c}$.
    Repeat. 
    Else go to Step~$2$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Reinsert 1-runs at stored indices

nodes.name: Decoding Step 2
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 2:}
    Let~$i$ be the decimal representation of~$(c_{3k+1},c_{3k+2},\ldots,c_{3k+\lceil \log (3k) \rceil})$. 
    Delete~$(c_{3k},c_{3k+2},\ldots,$ $c_{3k+\lceil \log k\rceil+3})$ from~$\mathbf{c}$ and insert~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil+5}$ at location~$i$ of~$\mathbf{c}$.    
    Output~$\mathbf{c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Undo the initialization step

nodes.name: Decoder termination
nodes.statement: Note that in the encoding procedure, the appended subsequence in the Initialization Step ends with a~$0$. The appended subsequence in Step~$1$ ends with a~$1$. Hence the algorithm stops when~$\mathbf{c}_{3k+\lceil \log k\rceil+3}=0$ and the subsequence~$(c_{3k},c_{3k+2},\ldots,$ $c_{3k+\lceil \log k\rceil+3})$ is deleted.
nodes.statement_short: Final bits signal which step to undo

nodes.name: Decoder reverses encoder
nodes.statement:
Similarly to the proof of correctness of decoding in Proposition~\ref{lemma:frequentpattern}, the decoding procedure exactly reverses the series of operations in the encoding procedure.
Let $T_{2,i}(\mathbf{c})$,~$i\in [0,I]$ be the sequence obtained after the~$i$-th deleting and appending operation in the encoding procedure, where
$I$ is the number of deleting and appending operations in total in the encoding procedure.
Then~$T_{2,i}(\mathbf{c})$ is the sequence obtained after the~$I-i$-th deleting and inserting operation in the decoding procedure. Therefore, the decoding procedure recovers the sequence~$\mathbf{c}$ after the~$I$-th operation.
nodes.statement_short: Decoding reverses the encoder as for $T_1$

nodes.name: Encoding procedure intro
nodes.statement:
We are now ready to present the encoding and decoding procedure for computing~$T(\mathbf{c})$.
The encoding procedure is as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Announce the encoder for $T$

nodes.name: Encoding: initialization
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Initialization:} Let~$T(\mathbf{c})=T_1(\mathbf{c})$.
    Append~$(\boldsymbol{0}^{3k},\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil +5})$ to the end of the sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})$. Let~$n'=n+2\lceil\log k\rceil+10$ (the length of~$T_1(\mathbf{c})$) and~$i=1$.
    Go to Step~$1$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Start from $T_1(\mathbf{c})$ and append $0^{3k}1^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$

nodes.name: Encoding Step 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 1:} If~$i\le \min\{n',n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+16-R\}$ and
    for every~$j\in [i,i+R-3k-\lceil \log k\rceil-4]$, there exists~$m\in [j,j+3k-1]$ such that~$(T(\mathbf{c})_m,T(\mathbf{c})_{m+1},\ldots,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{m+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})=\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil +5}$, split~$(T(\mathbf{c})_i,T(\mathbf{c})_{i+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{i+R-1})$ into~$(\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil)$ blocks~$\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$ of length~$3k+\lceil \log k \rceil +4$. Delete~$(\mathbf{b}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +8+\lceil\log k\rceil})$ from~$T(\mathbf{c})$ and append~$(0,T_2(\mathbf{b}_2),T_2(\mathbf{b}_3),\ldots,T_2(\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil+8+\lceil\log k\rceil}),i+3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+4,\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5},0)$ to the end of
    ~$T(\mathbf{c})$. Let~$n'=n'-R+6k+2\lceil\log k\rceil+8$ and~$i=1$. Repeat.
    Else go to Step~$2$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Compress a Property-2-violating window blockwise with $T_2$ and append it

nodes.name: Encoding Step 2
nodes.statement_short: Advance $i$ or output

nodes.name: Length invariant
nodes.statement:
The length of~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps constant and is~$n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15$. 
The subsequence~$T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15}$ are appended bits. 
The subsequence~$T(\mathbf{c})_1,\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n'}$ consists of the remaining bits in~$T(\mathbf{c})$ after deletions in Step~$1$. Note that~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ is not deleted.
nodes.statement_short: Length is $n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15$; appended bits kept

nodes.name: Invariant on the boundary
nodes.statement:
We show that~$T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+3k}=\boldsymbol{0}^{3k}$ and that either~$T(\mathbf{c})_{n'-\lceil\log k\rceil-4},\ldots,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{n'}=\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ or~$T(\mathbf{c})_{n'-\lceil\log k\rceil-5},\ldots,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{n'-1}=\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$. 
The proof is based on induction on the number~$r$ of deleting operations in Step~$1$ that have been done.
According to Proposition~\ref{lemma:frequentpattern}, the claim holds after the Initialization Step and hence after~$r=0$ deleting operations. Suppose the claim holds after~$r$ deleting operations and we have that~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+3k})=\boldsymbol{0}^{3k}$. Then in the~$r+1$-deleting operation in Step~$1$, the "if" condition only holds when~$i\le n'-R$. Otherwise, for~$j=n'\in [i,i+R-1]$, we have that~$(c_m,c_{m+1},\ldots,$ $c_{m+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil +5}$ for every~$m\in [j,j+3k-1]$, contradicting to the "if" condition. Furthermore, note that the bits~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{i+R-3k-\lceil\log k\rceil-4},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ after block~$\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil+9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$ are not deleted in the deleting operation.
Hence the bits~$T(\mathbf{c})_{n'-\lceil\log k\rceil-5},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15}$ stay in~$T(\mathbf{c})$. Therefore, the claim holds after~$r+1$-th deleting operation and holds after any number of deleting operations.
nodes.statement_short: Show the boundary invariant by induction on deletions

nodes.name: Induction on r
nodes.statement: The proof is based on induction on the number~$r$ of deleting operations in Step~$1$ that have been done.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on the number of deleting operations

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: According to Proposition~\ref{lemma:frequentpattern}, the claim holds after the Initialization Step and hence after~$r=0$ deleting operations.
nodes.statement_short: Holds after initialization by Proposition 4

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
Suppose the claim holds after~$r$ deleting operations and we have that~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+3k})=\boldsymbol{0}^{3k}$. Then in the~$r+1$-deleting operation in Step~$1$, the "if" condition only holds when~$i\le n'-R$. Otherwise, for~$j=n'\in [i,i+R-1]$, we have that~$(c_m,c_{m+1},\ldots,$ $c_{m+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil +5}$ for every~$m\in [j,j+3k-1]$, contradicting to the "if" condition. Furthermore, note that the bits~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{i+R-3k-\lceil\log k\rceil-4},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ after block~$\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil+9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$ are not deleted in the deleting operation.
Hence the bits~$T(\mathbf{c})_{n'-\lceil\log k\rceil-5},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15}$ stay in~$T(\mathbf{c})$. Therefore, the claim holds after~$r+1$-th deleting operation and holds after any number of deleting operations.
nodes.statement_short: A deletion only happens far from the boundary, so the invariant persists

nodes.name: Property 1 holds
nodes.statement:
We now show that~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$.

From Proposition~\ref{lemma:frequentpattern}, the initial sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})=(T_1(\mathbf{c}),\boldsymbol{0}^{3k},\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5})$ satisfies Property~$1$. 
We prove that~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps Property~$1$ after the deleting and inserting operations. 
Note that the deleting operation does not delete~$\mathbf{b}_1$ and~$\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$, which both contain~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ as a subsequence. Hence the deleting operation do not change the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns before block~$\mathbf{b}_1$ and after~$\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$. Since the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns in~$(\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil})$ is at most~$6k+2\lceil\log k\rceil+8\le B-\lceil\log k\rceil-5$, the sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps Property~$1$ after a deleting operation. Moreover, the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns in the
appended bits~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ is at most~$R-6k-2\lceil\log k\rceil-8\le B-\lceil\log k\rceil-5$. Note that the appended bits are not deleted in the deleting operations. Hence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps Property~$1$ after an inserting operation and we conclude that the output~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property 1

nodes.name: Initial sequence
nodes.statement: From Proposition~\ref{lemma:frequentpattern}, the initial sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})=(T_1(\mathbf{c}),\boldsymbol{0}^{3k},\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5})$ satisfies Property~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: Initially Property 1 holds by Proposition 4

nodes.name: Property 1 preserved
nodes.statement:
We prove that~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps Property~$1$ after the deleting and inserting operations. 
Note that the deleting operation does not delete~$\mathbf{b}_1$ and~$\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$, which both contain~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ as a subsequence. Hence the deleting operation do not change the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns before block~$\mathbf{b}_1$ and after~$\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$. Since the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns in~$(\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil})$ is at most~$6k+2\lceil\log k\rceil+8\le B-\lceil\log k\rceil-5$, the sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps Property~$1$ after a deleting operation. Moreover, the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns in the
appended bits~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ is at most~$R-6k-2\lceil\log k\rceil-8\le B-\lceil\log k\rceil-5$. Note that the appended bits are not deleted in the deleting operations. Hence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps Property~$1$ after an inserting operation and we conclude that the output~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: Deleting and inserting operations preserve Property 1

nodes.name: Boundary blocks kept
nodes.statement: Note that the deleting operation does not delete~$\mathbf{b}_1$ and~$\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$, which both contain~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ as a subsequence.
nodes.statement_short: Blocks $\mathbf{b}_1$ and the last block, which contain runs, are kept

nodes.name: Distances outside unchanged
nodes.statement: Hence the deleting operation do not change the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns before block~$\mathbf{b}_1$ and after~$\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil}$.
nodes.statement_short: Run distances outside the window unchanged

nodes.name: Deleting preserves
nodes.statement: Since the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns in~$(\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil +9+\lceil\log k\rceil})$ is at most~$6k+2\lceil\log k\rceil+8\le B-\lceil\log k\rceil-5$, the sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps Property~$1$ after a deleting operation.
nodes.statement_short: Run distance across the window at most $B-\lceil\log k\rceil-5$

nodes.name: Inserting preserves
nodes.statement:
Moreover, the distance of consecutive~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ patterns in the
appended bits~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ is at most~$R-6k-2\lceil\log k\rceil-8\le B-\lceil\log k\rceil-5$. Note that the appended bits are not deleted in the deleting operations. Hence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ keeps Property~$1$ after an inserting operation and we conclude that the output~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$.
nodes.statement_short: Appended bits also have close runs; Property 1 holds

nodes.name: Property 2 holds
nodes.statement:
Next, we prove that~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$2$. According to the encoding procedure, for any~$i\in [1,\min\{n',n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+16-R\}]$, there exists some~$j\in[i,i+R-3k-\lceil \log k\rceil-4]$, such that~$(T(\mathbf{c})_m,T(\mathbf{c})_{m+1},\ldots,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{m+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil +5}$ for every~$m\in [j,j+3k-1]$.  
Note that the appended bits~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ are not deleted. Hence for~$i\in [n'+1,n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+16-R]$, the interval~$[i,i+R-1]$ contains a subinterval~$[j,j+3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+3]$ such that~$T(\mathbf{c})_{j}=0$ and~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{j+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{j+3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+3})=T_2(\mathbf{b}_2)$, where~$\mathbf{b}_2\in\{0,1\}^{3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+4}$ contains the~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ pattern. Then~$(T(\mathbf{c})_m,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{m+1},\ldots,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{m+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil +5}$ for every~$m\in [j,j+3k-1]$. Therefore, the sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$2$. According to Proposition~\ref{lemma:property1and2}, we conclude that~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$ and Property~$2$ and is~\emph{$k$ dense}.
nodes.statement_short: Show $T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property 2

nodes.name: Remaining part
nodes.statement: According to the encoding procedure, for any~$i\in [1,\min\{n',n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+16-R\}]$, there exists some~$j\in[i,i+R-3k-\lceil \log k\rceil-4]$, such that~$(T(\mathbf{c})_m,T(\mathbf{c})_{m+1},\ldots,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{m+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil +5}$ for every~$m\in [j,j+3k-1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining bits satisfy Property 2 by the stopping rule

nodes.name: Appended part
nodes.statement: Note that the appended bits~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{n'+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ are not deleted. Hence for~$i\in [n'+1,n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+16-R]$, the interval~$[i,i+R-1]$ contains a subinterval~$[j,j+3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+3]$ such that~$T(\mathbf{c})_{j}=0$ and~$(T(\mathbf{c})_{j+1},\ldots,T(\mathbf{c})_{j+3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+3})=T_2(\mathbf{b}_2)$, where~$\mathbf{b}_2\in\{0,1\}^{3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+4}$ contains the~$\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil\log k\rceil+5}$ pattern. Then~$(T(\mathbf{c})_m,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{m+1},\ldots,$ $T(\mathbf{c})_{m+\lceil \log k \rceil +4})\ne\boldsymbol{1}^{\lceil \log k \rceil +5}$ for every~$m\in [j,j+3k-1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Appended windows contain a $T_2$-encoded run-free block

nodes.name: Conclude k dense
nodes.statement: Therefore, the sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$2$. According to Proposition~\ref{lemma:property1and2}, we conclude that~$T(\mathbf{c})$ satisfies Property~$1$ and Property~$2$ and is~\emph{$k$ dense}.
nodes.statement_short: Property 2 holds; by Proposition 3, $T(\mathbf{c})$ is $k$ dense

nodes.name: Complexity
nodes.statement: Since either~$i$ increases from~$1$ to~$n'$ or~$n'$ decreases in the encoding procedure, the procedure terminates within~$O(n^2)$ iterations. Each iteration takes~$O(k\log kR)$ time to check a violation of Property~$2$. Hence the complexity is at most~$O(n^2k^2\log k(\log n))$. Therefore, the total complexity is~$poly(n,k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomial complexity

nodes.name: Decoding procedure intro
nodes.statement_short: Announce the decoder

nodes.name: Decoding: initialization
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Initialization:} Let~$\mathbf{c}=T(\mathbf{c})$ and go to Step~$1$. 
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Start from $T(\mathbf{c})$

nodes.name: Decoding Step 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 1:} If~$c_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15}=0$, let~$i$ be the decimal representation of~$(c_{n+3k+2\lceil\log k\rceil+10-\lceil \log n\rceil},$
    \newline
    $c_{n+3k+2\lceil\log k\rceil+11-\lceil \log n\rceil},\ldots,c_{n+3k+2\lceil\log k\rceil+9})$. Split~$(c_{n+9k+5\lceil\log k\rceil+25-R},\ldots,c_{n+3k+2\lceil\log k\rceil+9-\lceil \log n\rceil})$ into 
    \newline
    $\lceil \log n\rceil+7+\lceil\log k\rceil$ blocks~$(\mathbf{b}'_1,\ldots,\mathbf{b}'_{\lceil \log n\rceil+7+\lceil\log k\rceil})$ of length~$3k+\lceil\log k\rceil+3$. Compute~$\mathbf{b}_j=T^{-1}_2(\mathbf{b}'_j)$ for~$j\in [1,\lceil \log n\rceil+7+\lceil\log k\rceil]$, where~$T^{-1}_2(\mathbf{b}'_j)$ is obtained by applying~$T_2$ decoder (Proposition~\ref{lemma:3kto3kminus1}) on~$\mathbf{b}'_j$.
    Delete \newline 
    $(c_{n+9k+5\lceil\log k\rceil+24-R},\ldots,$ $c_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ from~$\mathbf{c}$ and insert~$\mathbf{b}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{b}_{\lceil \log n\rceil+7+\lceil\log k\rceil}$ at location~$i$ of~$\mathbf{c}$.
    Repeat. 
    Else delete~$(c_{n+2\lceil\log k\rceil+11},\ldots,c_{n+3k+3\lceil\log k\rceil+15})$ and output~$T^{-1}_1(\mathbf{c})$.
nodes.statement_short: Decode appended windows with the $T_2$ decoder and reinsert; finally apply $T_1^{-1}$

nodes.name: Decoder termination
nodes.statement: According to the encoding procedure, the inserted bits end with a~$1$ entry in the Initialization Step and with a~$0$ entry in Step~$1$. Note that the inserted bits are not deleted in the encoding procedure. Hence the decoding algorithm stops when an ending~$1$ entry is detected.
nodes.statement_short: Final bit signals when to stop

nodes.name: Decoder reverses encoder
nodes.statement:
Similarly to the 
to the proof of correctness of decoding in Proposition~\ref{lemma:frequentpattern} and Proposition~\ref{lemma:3kto3kminus1}, the decoding procedure exactly reverses the series of operations in the encoding procedure. Therefore, the decoding procedure decodes the sequence~$\mathbf{c}$ correctly. The proof is done.
nodes.statement_short: Decoding reverses the encoder

nodes.name: Redundancy count
nodes.statement:
The length of~$R'(\mathbf{c})$ is~$N_1=8k\log (n+3k+3\lceil \log k\rceil +15)+o(\log (n+3k+3\lceil \log k\rceil +15))=8k\log n +o(\log n)$. The length of~$R''(\mathbf{c})$ is~$N_2=2k(k+1)(N_1/\lceil \log n\rceil )\log \log n=o(\log n)$. 
Therefore, the redundancy of~$\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{c})$ is~$N_1+N_2=8k\log n+o(\log n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Redundancy $N_1+N_2=8k\log n+o(\log n)$

nodes.name: Two recovery claims
nodes.statement:
Let~$N=n+8k\log n +o(\log n)$ be the length of~$\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{c})$. To show that~$\mathbf{c}$ can be recovered from a length~$N-k$ subsequence~$\mathbf{d}$ of~$\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{c})$, we prove that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The redundancy~$R'(\mathbf{c})$ can be recovered from~$k$ deletions with the help of~$R''(\mathbf{c})$.
    \item The sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ can be recovered from~$k$ deletions with the help of~$R'(\mathbf{c})$.
\end{enumerate}
Note that~$(d_{n+N_1+1},\ldots,d_{n+N_1+N_2-k})$ is a length~$N_2-k$ subsequence of~$R''(\mathbf{c})$. Since~$R''(\mathbf{c})$ is a~$k$ deletion code protecting~$H(R'(\mathbf{c}))$, the hash function $H(R'(\mathbf{c}))$ can be recovered from~$(d_{n+N_1+1},\ldots,d_{n+N_1+N_2-k})$.
Moreover,~$(d_{n+1},\ldots,$ $d_{n+N_1-k})$ is a length~$N_1-k$ subsequence of~$R'(\mathbf{c})$. From Lemma~\ref{lemma:hash} the hash function~$H(R'(\mathbf{c}))$ protects~$R'(\mathbf{c})$ from~$k$ deletions. Hence~$(1)$ holds. 

We now prove~$(2)$. According to Lemma~\ref{lemma:protectingpattern}, the \emph{synchronization vector}~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(T(\mathbf{c}))$ can be recovered from~$M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(T(\mathbf{c})))) $ $\bmod p(T(\mathbf{c}))$ and~$p(T(\mathbf{c}))$. Since by Lemma~\ref{lemma:transformation},~$T(\mathbf{c})$ is a~\emph{$k$ dense} sequence. Hence from Lemma~\ref{lemma:recoverforkdense}, it can be recovered based on~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(T(\mathbf{c}))$ and~$Hash_k(T(\mathbf{c}))$. Finally, the sequence~$\mathbf{c}$
can be recovered from~$T(\mathbf{c})$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:transformation}. Hence~$(2)$ holds and~$\mathbf{c}$ can be recovered.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce decoding to two claims: recover $R'$, then $T(\mathbf{c})$

nodes.name: Claim (1)
nodes.statement:
The redundancy~$R'(\mathbf{c})$ can be recovered from~$k$ deletions with the help of~$R''(\mathbf{c})$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: $R'$ recoverable via $R''$

nodes.name: Claim (2)
nodes.statement: The sequence~$T(\mathbf{c})$ can be recovered from~$k$ deletions with the help of~$R'(\mathbf{c})$.
nodes.statement_short: $T(\mathbf{c})$ recoverable via $R'$

nodes.name: Proof of (1)
nodes.statement:
Note that~$(d_{n+N_1+1},\ldots,d_{n+N_1+N_2-k})$ is a length~$N_2-k$ subsequence of~$R''(\mathbf{c})$. Since~$R''(\mathbf{c})$ is a~$k$ deletion code protecting~$H(R'(\mathbf{c}))$, the hash function $H(R'(\mathbf{c}))$ can be recovered from~$(d_{n+N_1+1},\ldots,d_{n+N_1+N_2-k})$.
Moreover,~$(d_{n+1},\ldots,$ $d_{n+N_1-k})$ is a length~$N_1-k$ subsequence of~$R'(\mathbf{c})$. From Lemma~\ref{lemma:hash} the hash function~$H(R'(\mathbf{c}))$ protects~$R'(\mathbf{c})$ from~$k$ deletions. Hence~$(1)$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Repetition code recovers $H(R')$, then Lemma 5 recovers $R'$

nodes.name: Proof of (2)
nodes.statement:
We now prove~$(2)$. According to Lemma~\ref{lemma:protectingpattern}, the \emph{synchronization vector}~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(T(\mathbf{c}))$ can be recovered from~$M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(T(\mathbf{c})))) $ $\bmod p(T(\mathbf{c}))$ and~$p(T(\mathbf{c}))$. Since by Lemma~\ref{lemma:transformation},~$T(\mathbf{c})$ is a~\emph{$k$ dense} sequence. Hence from Lemma~\ref{lemma:recoverforkdense}, it can be recovered based on~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(T(\mathbf{c}))$ and~$Hash_k(T(\mathbf{c}))$. Finally, the sequence~$\mathbf{c}$
can be recovered from~$T(\mathbf{c})$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:transformation}. Hence~$(2)$ holds and~$\mathbf{c}$ can be recovered.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2 recovers the synchronization vector, Lemma 3 recovers $T(\mathbf{c})$, Lemma 4 recovers $\mathbf{c}$

nodes.name: Complexity
nodes.statement: The encoding complexity of~$\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{c})$ is~$O(n^{2k+1})$, which comes from brute fore searching for ~$p(T(\mathbf{c}))$. The decoding compliexity is~$O(n^k+1)$, which comes from brute force searching for the correct~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(T(\mathbf{c}))$, given~$M(f(\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(T(\mathbf{c})))) \bmod p(T(\mathbf{c}))$ and~$p(T(\mathbf{c}))$.
nodes.statement_short: Brute-force searches give the encoding and decoding complexity

nodes.name: Synchronization vector of d
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 1:} Let~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})\in\{0,1\}^{n-k}$ be the \emph{synchronization vector} of~$\mathbf{d}$.
    Recall that the locations of~$1$ entries in~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{c})$ are~$1\le t_1<\ldots<t_J\le n$. Let~$t_0=0$ and~$t_{J+1}=n+1$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})$

nodes.name: Candidate blocks
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 2:} Let~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})_0=\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})_{n+1-k}=1$. For each~$j\in [0,J]$, if there exist two numbers~$i_j\in [t_j-k,t_j]$ and~$i_{j+1}\in [t_{j+1}-k,t_{j+1}]$ such that~$\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})_{i_{j}}=\mathbbold{1}_{sync}(\mathbf{d})_{i_{j+1}}=1$,  let~$\mathbf{a}'_j=(d_{i_j+1},d_{i_j+2},\ldots,
    d_{i_{j+1}-1})$. Else let~$\mathbf{a}'_j=0$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Cut $\mathbf{d}$ between synchronization 1's near $t_j$ into candidate blocks $\mathbf{a}'_j$

nodes.name: Reed-Solomon decoding
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Step 3:} Apply the Reed-Solomon decoder to recover~$H(\mathbf{a}_j)$ ($\mathbf{a}_j$ defined in~\eqref{equation:aj}),~$j\in [0,J]$,  from~$(H(\mathbf{a}'_0),$ $\ldots,H(\mathbf{a}'_J),$ $Hash_k(\mathbf{c}))$.
    \item
nodes.statement_short: Recover all block hashes $H(\mathbf{a}_j)$

nodes.name: Recover blocks
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 4:} Let~$\mathbf{b}_j=(d_{t_j+1},d_{t_{j}+2},\ldots,d_{t_{j+1}-k-1})$, recover~$\mathbf{a}_j$ by using~$\mathbf{b}_j$ and~$H(\mathbf{a}_j)$. Then recover~$\mathbf{c}$ from~$\mathbf{a}_j$,~$j\in[0,J]$.
nodes.statement_short: Recover each block from its subsequence and hash, then $\mathbf{c}$
